title: I Disagree!
subtitle: Four arguments, from polite to firm
review: Text by the author; notes and questions written by Claude: check them. No Burmese yet.
intro: The heating, a suitcase with six pairs of shoes, some missing chocolate and pineapple on pizza: four small arguments between Emma and Lucas. Listen for how the disagreement goes from polite to firm, and how they end it.

lines.text: It's cold in here, isn't it?
I wouldn't say that. It's seventy-two degrees.
lines.note: I wouldn't say that: a polite way to disagree. Seventy-two degrees Fahrenheit is about 22°C.

lines.text: I don't quite agree. I'm wearing three sweaters.
lines.note: I don't quite agree = I agree only partly.

lines.text: I see what you mean, but heating is expensive.
That's debatable. Getting sick isn't cheap either.
lines.note: That's debatable = I'm not sure that's true.

lines.text: With all due respect, that third sweater is mine.
lines.note: With all due respect is formal: it comes before a firm disagreement. Here it is a joke.

lines.text: It was just lying on the couch.
I was wearing it.
Six pairs of shoes? We're only going away for two days.
Not exactly. Two and a half days.
Are you going to wear all of them?
I don't think so.
lines.note: I don't think so: a soft no.

lines.text: Then you don't really need them all.
Yeah, but I don't know which ones I'll wear yet.
lines.note: Yeah, but… accepts the point, then objects.

lines.text: I get it, but the suitcase won't close.
lines.note: I get it = I understand. Won't close: it refuses to close.

lines.text: I beg to differ. Sit on it.
lines.note: I beg to differ: formal and old-fashioned for 'I disagree'. Used here for fun.

lines.text: You're the one who finished the chocolate.
lines.note: You're the one who… = it was you.

lines.text: Not at all!
lines.note: Not at all!: a strong no.

lines.text: There were three squares left last night.
That's not true. There were two.
So you counted them.
That's beside the point.
lines.note: Beside the point: it does not answer the question.

lines.text: You've got chocolate on your chin.
You're wrong. It's… coffee.
lines.note: You're wrong is direct. Use it with people you know well.

lines.text: I don't think so. Coffee doesn't smell like hazelnuts.
lines.note: Smell like: have the smell of.

lines.text: Pineapple on pizza is a crime.
To each their own. I love it.
lines.note: To each their own: people like different things.

lines.text: It's a fruit! On a pizza!
Tomatoes are fruit too.
You've lost me there.
lines.note: You've lost me there = I can't follow your argument.

lines.text: Well, we'll just have to agree to disagree.
lines.note: Agree to disagree: accept that we think differently, and stop arguing.

lines.text: You're right. Let's not argue about it. Can I try some?
The pineapple?
Just to make sure.
lines.note: Just to make sure = just to check.

notes: Polite: I wouldn't say that, I don't quite agree, That's debatable.
Yeah, but… and I get it, but… accept the point first, then give the objection.
Firm: Not at all!, That's not true, You're wrong. They are direct: use them with friends and family.
That's beside the point rejects an argument that does not answer the question.
To end an argument: To each their own, We'll have to agree to disagree, Let's not argue about it.
I beg to differ and With all due respect are formal. Friends use them as a joke.

questions.q: Lucas politely disagrees that it is cold. What does he say?
questions.why: I wouldn't say that is a polite, gentle way to disagree.

questions.q: Emma accepts Lucas's point about the shoes, then objects. How does she begin?
questions.why: Yeah, but… accepts the point, then adds the objection.

questions.q: Lucas says counting the chocolate does not matter. What does he say?
questions.why: That's beside the point = that does not answer the question.

questions.q: Emma ends the pizza argument without changing her mind. What does she say?
options: We'll just have to agree to disagree.
questions.why: Agree to disagree = accept that we think differently, and stop arguing.
